title: Reading history: log, graphs, and diffs
explanation:
`git log` lists commits newest first, each with its id (SHA-1), author, date, and message. A few options make it much more useful:

- `--oneline` — one short line per commit; ideal for scanning.
- `--graph` — draws the branch and merge structure as ASCII art beside the log.
- `-p` (or `--patch`) — shows the diff each commit introduced; `-2` limits output to the last two commits.

```bash
git log --oneline --graph      # compact history of the current branch, with merges drawn
git log -p -2                  # the last two commits with their patches
git log --stat                 # which files each commit touched
```

Diffs answer "what changed?" at different levels: `git diff` compares your working directory with the index, `git diff --staged` compares the index with the last commit, and `git log -p` shows what each recorded commit changed. Inspecting before acting — especially before merging, rebasing, or resetting — is the cheapest way to avoid mistakes.
keyIdeas: `-p` shows each commit's patch; `-N` limits how many.
Inspect before you merge, rebase, or reset.

workedExample.problem: A repository has `trunk` and a branch `cocoa` with two extra commits. Show a compact graph of both branches, then show only the last commit's patch, and list which files `cocoa` changed compared with `trunk`.
steps: Name both branches to include their history: `git log --oneline --graph trunk cocoa`.
`git log -p -1 cocoa` prints the newest commit on `cocoa` with its diff.
`git diff --stat trunk cocoa` summarises the file-level differences between the two branch tips.

Run it in a throwaway folder:
```sh
git init -q -b trunk shop && cd shop
printf 'tea\n' > menu.md && git add menu.md && git commit -q -m 'Add menu'
git switch -q -c cocoa
printf 'cocoa\n' >> menu.md && git commit -q -am 'Add cocoa to menu'
printf 'cocoa 5\n' > prices.md && git add prices.md && git commit -q -m 'Price cocoa'
git log --oneline --graph trunk cocoa
[ "$(git log --oneline trunk..cocoa | wc -l)" -eq 2 ]          # two commits only on cocoa
git log -p -1 cocoa | grep -q '^+cocoa 5'                        # the patch of the newest commit
[ "$(git diff --name-only trunk cocoa | sort | tr '\n' ' ')" = 'menu.md prices.md ' ]
echo ok
```
workedExample.answer: The graph shows `Price cocoa` and `Add cocoa to menu` above `Add menu`; the last patch adds `cocoa 5`; `cocoa` differs from `trunk` in `menu.md` and `prices.md`.

pitfalls: Reading plain `git log` output for a branchy history instead of adding `--graph`.
Using `git diff` to see what was committed — it compares the working directory with the index, not commits.
Running a destructive command (reset, rebase) without first checking the log for what will move.

citations.quote: By default, with no arguments, git log lists the commits made in that repository in reverse chronological order; that is, the most recent commits show up first.
--graph Display an ASCII graph of the branch and merge history beside the log output.
One of the more helpful options is -p or --patch, which shows the difference (the patch output) introduced in each commit. You can also limit the number of log entries displayed
--stat Show statistics for files modified in each commit.
That command compares what is in your working directory with what is in your staging area.
